blocks.text: The chapter begins with a commission to Jonah and immediately contrasts it with his flight toward Tarshish. Jonah 4 later connects that flight with what Jonah knows about Jehovah’s graciousness, but it does not fully explain his inner motive. The matching name and patronymic in 2 Kings 14:25 identify a related prophetic figure, yet they do not establish that this figure authored the present third-person narrative.

Tarshish’s precise location is uncertain; proposals range from a place in Iberia to other western maritime associations. More importantly for the scene, fleeing “from the presence of Jehovah” need not mean Jonah thinks Jehovah has no power over the sea. It can describe his refusal of the commission or departure from the sphere to which he was sent. The sailors’ movement from praying to their own gods to fearing Jehovah, sacrificing, and making vows is clear in the story, while the exact nature or permanence of their response remains open.

The lot identifies Jonah as the person connected with the crisis within this narrative; it is not presented as a general religious method for making decisions. Likewise, Jonah’s request to be thrown into the sea does not settle whether he acts from responsibility, despair, self-sacrifice, avoidance, or another motive. The sailors first try hard to reach land, then appeal to Jehovah before acting—details that keep their conduct from being reduced to a simple stereotype.

The narrative calls Jonah to proclaim Jehovah’s word, but it never itself uses the noun “prophet” for him. Numbering also differs across traditions: the fish appointment commonly printed as Jonah 1:17 begins chapter 2 in Masoretic numbering. Awareness of that difference helps prevent confusion when comparing references to the fish and Jonah’s prayer.

The text says that Jehovah appoints a great fish to swallow Jonah. It does not identify the creature’s species, explain how it sustains him, or say that Jonah dies inside it. The “three days and three nights” should therefore be read first as the narrated duration, rather than as material for reconstructing fish biology or an exact chronology.

Across the whole book, Jonah became the haftarah—the prophetic reading—for the Minḥah, or afternoon, service of Yom Kippur in Jewish liturgy. That reception has made the book’s questions of repentance, mercy, justice, and resistance especially prominent in Jewish communal reading.
